result:
Solution 3 is correct on its answer. Solutions 1 and 2 are not, but I did not prove the characterisation in full.

**Solution 2.** The condition n² ≡ 1 (mod 3) is necessary, but I could not make it sufficient. I tried to build n = 5 by hand. Staircase growth along the diagonal cannot fill the last cells of the top row and right column. Colouring (2,4) always colours a neighbouring cell as well, and that leaves (1,5), (2,5) and (3,5) with no square that has exactly one black cell. I did not enumerate every sequence, but every attempt failed. Solution 2 also asserts sufficiency without any argument, so I reject it.

**Solution 1.** Its rule is unsupported and calls n = 7, 10, 11 and so on feasible with no construction. It rests on the same unproven claim of sufficiency as Solution 2, so I reject it.

**Solution 3.** The doubling construction for n = 2^k is sound. Fill the top-left quadrant recursively. The 2×2 square at the centre of the board then has exactly one black cell, the inner corner of that quadrant. Colouring that square seeds an inner corner in each of the other three quadrants. By symmetry each quadrant then fills recursively, so every power of 2 works. I also checked n = 3 by hand and it fails. My n = 5 attempts failed too. The claim that only powers of 2 work is plausible and consistent with these checks, though the non-existence argument in the solution is only sketched. This gives the sum 2²⁰ − 1 = 1048575, which I accept.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: ACCEPT
